author: suburbandad_
content:
this is timely.  I am looking at the eager secured-trie path walk in zesu pr 205 (https://github.com/Consensys-Incorporated/zesu/pull/205)  and am trying to figure out why we would care about malformed but not accessed nodes.  the block producer would have to pay (presumably) for the proof of the oversized/unused malformed nodes.

I'd go one further and get rid of the local-node check.  If we are going to allow malformed but unread nodes at depth, why would we bother with rejecting oversize nodes higher in the trie (such that we would see their cumulative nibble path exceeds 64)

author: suburbandad_
content:
There could be attacks I am not envisioning that would leverage "unvisited junk" in the witness.  

Whereas the eager trie walk has a verifiable cost.  Zesu has been doing a lazy trie walk and verification on read.  We have been rejecting oversize paths on read as INVALID_WITNESS, but if it is never read, we never reject.

for us: 
 naive eager walk costs on average an additional +14% steps
 inline rlp reading, stackifying gets it down to an average +6.6% steps
 further, adding a presence table (32 bytes * n nodes) gets avg steps down to +2.2%

There is a code complexity cost also.  And it leaves me wondering - are we just doing this so that we can spec a simple eager walk algorithm?
